extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students/scholars of poetics/literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragedy and epic narrative (diction, metre, unity, use of chorus, metaphor, marvellous, and narrative technique). Geared to poets/playwrights and critics studying classical poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be 'a member of the entirety' and participate in the performance as Sophocles rather than as Euripides makes it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the chorus part of the unified whole of the play, coordinated with the spectators and able to start or propagate emotions among the audience. Avoid assigning the chorus the chief share in the action or treating its songs as freely transferable between unrelated plays; choric material should be relevant to the particular tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Intelligence (speech-operations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction (intelligence) encompasses all operations for which Speech is the instrument: demonstration and refutation, arousing emotions (pity, fear, anger), exaggeration and depreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design speech to perform rhetorical operations appropriate to the scene—argue, refute, and evoke emotion. Study these operations in the broader science of Rhetoric; use diction to effect the intended emotional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show in action; produce in declamation
rubrics_metrics.description: In action, situations that are terrible, piteous, grand or plausible must be manifested without interpretation; in declamation they should be produced by the speaker and be the effect of his style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer dramatic enactment (showing) for scenes onstage so their qualities arise from the events themselves; reserve rhetorical ornament and explicit emotional production for spoken declamation. Avoid depending on a speaker's style to make inherently unconvincing actions produce the desired effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosodic control of letters and sounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of diction — letters, vowels, semi-vowels, mutes, combinations — differ by place of articulation, breathing, length, and intonation; all these differences should be studied in Prosody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to pronunciation, prosody, and prosodic licenses (lengthenings, contractions, intonations) as tools for poetic diction and metre; these are technical matters that affect rhythm, clarity, and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence of diction: clear and not common
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence of Diction is to be clear and not common: clearness comes from ordinary appellations; choiceness from extraordinary appellations (dialectic names, metaphors, protractions, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strike a balance between ordinary language (for clarity) and elevated/extraordinary language (for refinement). Using only ordinary words makes diction common; using only extraordinary forms produces riddles or gibberish. Moderate mixture preserves clarity and produces 'choiceness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excess of licences (dialectic names, metaphors, coined words)
rubrics_metrics.description: If all phrases are extraordinary (metaphors or dialectic names) the result will be a riddle or gibberish; moderation is necessary in employing metaphors, dialectic words, compounds, lengthenings, and other licences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical and lexical licences sparingly and purposefully; test substitutions of normal appellations to ensure the effect is felicitous. Excessive or ill-judged use of these devices renders language obscure or ludicrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should have the gift of original metaphor; this cannot be borrowed and is a sign of talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to coin metaphors that reveal genuine insight into likenesses between things. Original metaphors are higher-value ornaments than formulaic or borrowed figures and demonstrate creative vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of metaphor and how to use them
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor may apply a strange name from genus to species, species to genus, species to species, or by analogy; it can also substitute an improper appellation with a negation of one property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select metaphorical transfers suited to the relationship you want to convey (genus↔species, analogy). Consider associations and motion in images—images suggesting motion are more effective. Use analogy and substitution deliberately for clarity and impact (e.g., 'Dionysus's shield' as a transferred epithet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of appellation types to metre and genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Of appellations compounds are most suitable for dithyrambs, dialectic words for hexameters, metaphors for iambics; in hexameters many sorts may be employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match vocabulary types to metre and genre: heroic/hexametric poetry tolerates and benefits from dialectic names and varied licences; iambic (conversational) forms suit ordinary appellations, metaphors and euphemisms. Choose diction to fit metrical and genre expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use licences to serve metre but preserve clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthenings, dockings, and alterations of nouns produce choiceness while retaining clearness if related to ordinary appellations; the hexameter may require special vocabulary or alterations in word quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adjusting words for metre (e.g., lengthening vowels or altering forms), ensure alterations still resemble the ordinary appellation enough to maintain clarity. Don't sacrifice intelligibility for metrical convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story should be constructed to embrace one whole and complete chapter of life, with beginning, middle, and end, like one complete figure, producing the intended gratification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a single, causally unified episode or 'chapter' rather than an extended series of loosely connected events. Avoid turning the work into a monotonous chronicle; ensure incidents lead toward a single result or purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monotonous chronicles; select an artistic episode
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not produce monotonous chronicles that merely enumerate events within a period; instead, choose a single chapter (or episode) that forms a coherent artistic unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prune material from longer histories; use episodes effectively (as Homer does) rather than attempting to narrate an entire protracted sequence that lacks a single unifying end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic should embody tragedy's varieties (except music/presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic should have the same varieties as Tragedy (simple, complex, psychological, emotional) and the same factors except Music and Presentation — irony of fate, disclosure of mistaken identity, catastrophe, intelligence, and diction are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing epic, include structural and affective elements found in drama (reversal, recognition, emotional arcs) and maintain high-quality diction and thought; adapt presentation to the epic medium (narration) rather than stagecraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and metre suitability for epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic differs in length and metre from Tragedy: heroic metre (hexameter) is the suitable rhythm for lengthy narrative fiction, permitting stateliness and the admixture of dialectic names and metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use heroic metre for long narrative poems; exploit the narrative form to depict simultaneous portions of action (which stage performance cannot), but keep length bounded so beginning and end can be grasped as a unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marvellous and poetic justice — keep in background
rubrics_metrics.description: The marvellous (and poetic justice that intensifies it) should be introduced into the background rather than made an integral, foregrounded part of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If extraordinary or marvellous elements are necessary, prepare the audience and keep these elements peripheral to the causal core of the plot; foregrounding the unnatural risks disbelief or perceived impossibility, especially on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer plausible impossibility to unconvincing possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: You should prefer a plausible impossibility to an unconvincing possibility; the account should not be made up of unaccountable elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you must violate strict possibility, make the violation emotionally/plausibly convincing within the work's logic; avoid inserting arbitrary or unexplained miracles that undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use picturesque detail to induce belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Append picturesque details that naturally attend a fiction's assumed facts, because when people recognise consistent attendant details they are prone to accept the larger assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add small, plausible, law-of-nature-consistent details (the 'bath-scene' example) to lend verisimilitude to invented events. Such details exploit a psychological tendency to infer the primary fact from its natural accompaniments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimise authorial declamation; impersonate characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet/author ought to say as little as possible in his own person; rather, he should bring on the stage individual characters each with personality, avoiding prolonged declamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor dramatic impersonation and characterization over authorial exposition. Let characters' actions and speech reveal personality and plot, reserving narration for necessary transitions or framing, especially in epic where narrator's intrusion should be brief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety to prevent satiety
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety of scenes and character prevents satiety in long pieces; the narrative form allows simultaneous presentation of many portions to create variation of scenes and maintain interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure long works to vary scene, pace, and imagery; use narrative techniques that permit shifts of focus and tone so the audience does not grow weary of monotonous uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not transfer material indiscriminately between works
rubrics_metrics.description: Choric songs and other pieces of material have been transferred between works historically (a practice Agathon introduced), but this is unreasonable — e.g., transferring songs or scenes between plays is akin to transferring a speech or scene inappropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that set pieces (choral odes, speeches, scenes) belong organically to the work they appear in. Avoid recycling material without regard to its relevance to the specific plot, character, or unity of the piece.
